attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his signed Substack essay, arguing against Frazier and Thierer.

semantics.note: The firm part is 'will be absorbed as a cost of business', with no horizon. The draft keeps 'no serious argument' as an assertion and keeps the hedge 'likely tied'. Neither is scored on its own.

contract.note: Reading 'trivial' as not materially changing investment or competitiveness is an ordinary reading. The contradiction condition reaches into competitive effects, which the contract itself calls supporting assertion, but this does not change the result here.

evidence.note: Jan 2026 working paper. It discusses compliance costs and automation in general terms only: no realized company-specific costs and no measured effect on US-China competition.

reviews.rationale: This is an unqualified forecast with no deadline. The packet has no documented realized compliance costs for trillion-dollar firms and no study of competitive effects. No counterexample meets the early-resolution rule. The only item is general context, so the outcome is unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own parenthetical in his signed essay.

semantics.note: Faithful two-part observation: China had more national AI regulation, and its models caught up anyway. 'Not stopped' is correctly read as progress despite regulation, not as zero drag.

contract.note: Reading 'catching up' as narrowing the model-performance gap fits the nearby talk of models and leaderboards. Reading 'national regulation' as binding provider obligations is ordinary. The 2024 performance window is reasonable.

evidence.note: Peer-reviewed legal analysis (Jan 2025) of China's binding national rules on generative AI, algorithms and deep synthesis, including obligations on providers.
AI Index 2025 (Apr 2025): the gap on MMLU and HumanEval went from double digits in 2023 to near parity in 2024. The US still produces more notable models.
CRS report covering federal law as of May 2025: no broad federal authority to regulate AI. Published June 2025, before the cutoff, about the right period.

reviews.rationale: Legal sources show binding national AI rules on Chinese providers, while the US had no broad federal AI regulatory authority. Independent benchmark data show Chinese models reaching near parity in 2024 despite those rules. Both parts hold. The claim does not address the causal counterfactual.

attribution.note: Essay posted by Marcus and co-signed by state representatives. Marcus endorses it.

semantics.note: The draft leaves out 'all' and 'budget bill', which the contract restores. 'Major step backwards' is normative and correctly not scored.

contract.note: Strict reading of 'all' is anchored in the speaker's own repeated claim that states could not regulate AI 'in any way'. 'Almost nothing' has no threshold. Reading it as very limited substantive protection is ordinary.

evidence.note: Confirms the May 11, 2025 reconciliation text had a 10-year moratorium on state enforcement. Summary checked against the committee print. Later amendments are kept separate.
Contemporaneous markup transcript: even an opponent says exemptions exist, though 'very narrow'. So the literal 'all' overstates the provision.
CRS: no federal law as of May 2025 set up broad AI regulatory authority. Supports 'almost nothing', though targeted laws existed.
Official statement: Congress passed the Take It Down Act (Apr 2025), a targeted deepfake protection. It qualifies 'almost nothing' but does not refute it, and was unsigned at the time of the post.

reviews.rationale: Holds: a sweeping 10-year moratorium on state AI enforcement in a budget bill, and a thin congressional record (no broad authority; one targeted deepfake bill). Fails: the literal 'ban all state regulation', since the original text had narrow exemptions, which the contract says count.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his signed essay.

semantics.note: Faithful present-tense observation about national concentration on leaderboards.

contract.note: Reading 'dominated' as overwhelming national concentration of top positions, across more than one leaderboard, is ordinary. The May 1–14, 2025 window is reasonable.

evidence.note: LMArena, May 6, 2025: Google's Gemini 2.5 Pro was #1 in every arena. It gives top-ranked models only, not the national spread of leading positions.
Artificial Analysis, May 13, 2025: China's Kling 2.0 leads image-to-video. This is one category and does not settle the overall distribution.

reviews.rationale: The contract needs the country distribution of leading positions across representative leaderboards in May 2025. The packet has only category leaders: a US model swept LMArena, while a Chinese model led one video arena. That neither shows nor rules out overwhelming national concentration, so the outcome is unresolved.
